alternative: Rely on the JVM GC and scala.util.Using: Using.resource (or Using.Manager for several resources) releases in reverse order of acquisition, java.lang.ref.Cleaner covers library-owned resources, and immutable values (case classes, persistent collections) share without counts.
idiom_name: none - JVM GC owns lifetime; Using releases explicitly, values share without counts
implementation_notes: Scala runs on the JVM, where objects are traced rather than counted: there is no per-object count to embed and no way for a count field to force reclamation. What replaces the classic structure: immutable values for sharing - case-class copy and the persistent collections in scala.collection.immutable produce new values that reuse most of the old structure - and scala.util.Using for deterministic release of external resources: it wraps acquisition, use and release in a Try and, for several resources, releases them in reverse order of their creation; Using.resource is the variant that throws instead of returning Try. A hand-written counter is only protocol state.
code_sketch:
import scala.util.Using

val lines: Seq[String] =
  Using.resource(new BufferedReader(new FileReader("file.txt"))) { r =>
    Iterator.continually(r.readLine()).takeWhile(_ != null).toList
  }   // released on every exit path
pitfalls: Using.Manager releases in reverse acquisition order, and a resource registered with an outer manager can outlive the inner scope that logically owned it.
Immutable sharing removes the need for a count but not the need for release: external resources still require Using/AutoCloseable, and a value wrapping one must expose it.
A count kept in a var or AtomicInteger and read to decide behaviour is racy under the JVM memory model; use it for diagnostics at most.
